text:
“Do speak more quietly,” she said to him with a frightened look. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the New Heloise that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the New Heloise to a delighted Mademoiselle Amanda, and he was pleased with his own daring, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy expression. One of her lovers had appeared in the doorway of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and rolling his shoulders as he walked; he looked at Julien. At once, Julien’s imagination, always prone to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, assumed a self-assured expression, and looked at his rival very intently. As this rival lowered his head while casually pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been astonished by Julien’s eyes; after swallowing his glass of brandy in a single draught, he said a word to Amanda, thrust both hands into the side pockets of his heavy frock coat, and approached a billiard table, breathing noisily and looking at Julien. Julien rose, beside himself with anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little bundle and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it made a charming contrast with the artlessness of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the frock coat. She rose and, while pretending to be following with her eyes someone passing in the street, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? Of course he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have come from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she quickly added, her barmaid’s imagination supplying her with lies in abundance:

“Of course he looked at you, but that was when he was asking me who you were; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eyes followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice cry in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the next game.” He moved swiftly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:

“Come and pay me first,” she said to him.

That is fair, thought Julien; she is afraid I may leave without paying.

Amanda was as agitated as he was and very red; she gave him his change as slowly as she could, all the while repeating to him in a low voice:

“Leave the café this instant, or I shall not love you anymore; and yet I do love you dearly.”

Julien did leave, but slowly. Is it not my duty, he kept asking himself, to go and stare in my turn, breathing noisily, at that coarse fellow? This uncertainty kept him for an hour on the boulevard in front of the café; he watched to see whether his man would come out. He did not appear, and Julien went away.

He had been in Besançon for only a few hours, and already he had acquired something to reproach himself for. The old surgeon-major had once given him, despite his gout, a few fencing lessons; that was all the skill Julien could call upon in the service of his anger. But this difficulty would have been nothing if he had known how to become angry in any way other than by delivering a slap in the face; and if it came to blows, his rival, an enormous man, would have beaten him and then left him there.

For a poor devil like me, Julien told himself, without protectors and without money, there will not be much difference between a seminary and a prison; I must leave my civilian clothes at some inn, where I shall put my black coat back on. If I ever manage to get out of the seminary for a few hours, I shall be perfectly able, in my civilian clothes, to see Mademoiselle Amanda again. The reasoning was sound; but as Julien passed each inn, he did not dare enter any of them.

At last, as he passed the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs again, his anxious eyes met those of a stout woman, still fairly young, ruddy-faced, with a happy and cheerful air. He approached her and told her his story.

“Certainly, my pretty little abbé,” the landlady of the Ambassadeurs said to him, “I shall keep your civilian clothes for you and shall even have them dusted often. At this time of year, it is not good to leave a cloth coat untouched.” She took a key and led him herself to a room, instructing him to write down a list of what he was leaving.

“Good Lord! How handsome you look like that, Monsieur l’Abbé Sorel,” the stout woman said to him when he came down to the kitchen. “I am going to have a good dinner served to you, and,” she added in a low voice, “it will cost you only twenty sous instead of the fifty everyone else pays; for you must take good care of your little purse.”

“I have ten louis,” Julien replied with a certain pride.

“Oh! Good Lord!” the kindly landlady answered in alarm. “Do not speak so loudly; there are many bad characters in Besançon. You will have it stolen from you in no time. Above all, never go into the cafés; they are full of bad characters.”

“Really!” said Julien, to whom these words gave food for thought.

“Never go anywhere but my establishment; I shall have coffee made for you. Remember that you will always find a friend here and a good dinner for twenty sous—that is speaking plainly, I hope. Go and sit down at the table; I am going to serve you myself.”

“I could not eat,” Julien said to her. “I am too agitated; I am going to enter the seminary when I leave your establishment.”

The good woman did not let him leave until she had filled his pockets with provisions. At last Julien set off toward the terrible place; standing in her doorway, the landlady pointed out the way to him.
